title: Conversations that flow
cando: start, keep going and steer a natural conversation with people you don’t know well

about.text: In this lesson you go to a networking event and talk to people you have never met. You learn how to start a conversation, keep it going and steer it where you want it to go, with small words like actually, mind you and granted. Then you read an article about small talk at work and write a follow-up message to someone you met.
goals: Start a conversation with a stranger and find something you have in common.
Steer a conversation with actually, mind you, granted and anyway.
Use question tags and echo questions to check, agree and show interest.
Read an article about small talk at work and write a friendly follow-up message.
Meet new people at a networking event and arrange to stay in touch.

chapters.title: Meeting people you don't know
chapters.text:
Welcome to Level 4. In this first lesson, you are at a networking event.
It's a room full of people who work in the same area, or who want to meet people who do. Most of them don't know each other.
For many people, the hardest part is the first sentence. So start with an easy question. So, how do you know the organiser? What brings you here tonight?
Then listen for something you have in common: the same line of work, the same town, or a friend you both know.
Listen to Priya and Tomasz. They have never met before. Notice how they keep the conversation going, and how they move it from one topic to the next.

chapters.title: Small words that steer
chapters.text:
The grammar in this lesson is about small words that do a big job.
Actually corrects something gently, or adds a surprise. I'm not in sales, actually. I'm in logistics.
Mind you adds a but to what you have just said, without taking it back. The venue's lovely. Mind you, it's a bit noisy.
Granted agrees with part of a point before you argue on. Granted, it's a long way. But it's worth it.
Anyway moves the conversation on, or brings it back to the main topic. Anyway, what do you do?
The second point is tags. You work with Kwame, don't you? A tag checks something you think is true. If your voice goes down, you are fairly sure. If it goes up, you really want to know.
An echo question shows interest. I've just moved here from Leeds. Have you? What made you move?

chapters.title: Small talk at work
chapters.text:
In Section 3, you read an article about small talk at work. Some people think it's a waste of time. The writer disagrees.
She explains how a two-minute chat by the kettle helps colleagues trust each other, especially when a team works from home.
Read it once, quickly, for the main idea. Then read it again for the details: who says what, and what they suggest.
Then you write a short follow-up message to someone you met. Say where you met, mention something you talked about, and suggest a next step. Keep it friendly, and keep it short.

chapters.title: Networking in the live class
chapters.text:
Then it's your turn. In the live class, you meet three people. Start each conversation, find one thing you have in common, and arrange to follow up.
Don't worry about perfect grammar. Ask questions, listen to the answers, and use them in your next question.
Use the other person's name once or twice. It helps you remember it, and most people like hearing their own name.
If there's a silence, change the subject. What do you do when you're not working?
At the end, swap details and say what happens next. I'll drop you a line next week.

chapters.title: The book
chapters.text:
Last, you read a longer text linked to this lesson.
Read it once for the story. Then read it again and answer the questions. Notice how the people in it start a conversation, and how they keep it going.

warmup.prompt: You arrive at a work event and you don't know anyone there. What do you do first?
choices: get a drink and look around
talk to someone who is standing alone
warmup.note: There is no wrong answer. Many people feel awkward at first. Someone standing alone is often glad to talk, and the drinks table is a natural place to start a conversation.

conversation.title: At a networking event
conversation.setting: Priya works in marketing for a furniture company. At an evening event for local businesses, organised by Kwame Asante, she starts talking to Tomasz by the drinks table.
lines: Priya
Hi there. It's busy tonight, isn't it?
Tomasz
It certainly is. I'm Tomasz, by the way. So, how do you know Kwame?
Priya
I'm Priya. We used to work together at a bank, years ago. How about you?
Tomasz
I don't, actually. I came across the event online. I've just moved my business here from Leeds.
Priya
Have you? What line of work are you in?
Tomasz
Deliveries. We move furniture for shops, mostly. Lots of heavy lifting, and even more phone calls.
Priya
Really? Then we've got something in common. I do the marketing for Oakline Furniture.
Tomasz
You're joking! Your sofas are always the heaviest. Mind you, they're very well made.
Priya
I'll take that as a compliment! Leeds to here is a big move, though, isn't it?
Tomasz
It is. Granted, the rents are higher here. But there's far more work, and my wife's family live nearby.
Priya
That makes sense. Anyway, I mustn't keep you from the food. Have you got a business card?
Tomasz
Here you are. It's been really good to meet you, Priya.
Priya
You too. I'll drop you a line next week. We might have some work for you.

questions.a: They worked together at a bank.
wrong: They met at an event like this one.
Kwame delivers furniture for her company.
questions.why: Priya says: We used to work together at a bank, years ago.

questions.q: Why did Tomasz move his business?
questions.a: There's more work here, and his wife's family live nearby.
questions.why: Tomasz says the rents are higher, but there's far more work, and his wife's family live nearby.

questions.q: What does Priya say she will do next week?
questions.why: Priya says: I'll drop you a line next week. That means she will write to him.

phrases.text: So, how do you know Kwame?
phrases.use: An easy first question at an event: it asks about the host.

phrases.text: What line of work are you in?
phrases.use: Asking about someone's job in a relaxed way.

phrases.text: Then we've got something in common.
phrases.use: Pointing out a link, so the conversation has somewhere to go.

phrases.text: Mind you, they're very well made.
phrases.use: Adding a different point without taking back what you said.

phrases.text: Granted, the rents are higher here. But there's far more work.
phrases.use: Agreeing with part of a point, then going on with your own.
Moving a conversation on, or ending it politely.

phrases.text: It's been really good to meet you.
phrases.use: Saying goodbye to someone you have just met.

items.meaning: Meeting new people through work, so that you can help each other later on.
items.example: Most of my new clients came from networking, not from advertising.

items.meaning: To say or do something that helps people who have just met to relax and start talking.
items.example: He broke the ice by asking everyone about the terrible coffee.

items.meaning: If a name or a fact does this, it seems familiar, but you can't remember exactly why.
items.example: Tomasz Nowak? The name rings a bell. Have we met before?

items.meaning: Shared by two or more people. A friend of this kind is someone you both know.
items.example: We met through a mutual friend at a conference.

items.meaning: If two people have something like this, they share an interest, an experience or an opinion.
items.example: We've got a lot in common: we both grew up by the sea, and we both hate long meetings.

items.meaning: The kind of job someone does.
items.example: What line of work are you in?

items.meaning: A small, stiff piece of paper printed with your name, job and contact details. You give it to people you meet through work.
items.example: Here's my business card. My mobile number is on the back.

items.meaning: To find or meet something or someone by chance.
items.example: I came across your website while I was looking for a printer.

items.meaning: Uncomfortable and a little embarrassing, for example when nobody knows what to say.
items.example: There was an awkward silence after he mentioned the job cuts.

items.meaning: Liking to talk a lot, in a friendly and informal way.
items.example: The new receptionist is very chatty, so you'll know everyone by Friday.

items.meaning: Friendly and confident, and happy to meet and talk to new people.
items.example: You don't have to be outgoing to be good at networking.

items.meaning: Real and sincere, not pretended.
items.example: She showed a genuine interest in my work, so I enjoyed talking to her.

items.meaning: Something nice that you say about someone, their work or their things.
items.example: He paid me a compliment on my presentation.

items.meaning: To start talking more freely about yourself and your feelings.
items.example: After a few minutes, he opened up about how hard the move had been.

items.meaning: To start talking about something different, often because the first topic has become uncomfortable.
items.example: When the talk turned to salaries, I quickly changed the subject.

sound.title: Sounding interested
sound.explain: An echo question is very short: a helping verb and a pronoun, like Have you? or Is it? Your voice goes up at the end, and that tells the other person you are interested and want to hear more. A flat voice sounds bored, even with the right words. Listen, then say each group and each line.
groups: Have you? · Did you? · Are you?
Is it? · Was it? · Do they?
lines: I've just moved here from Leeds. — Have you? What made you move?
We used to work together. — Did you? Where was that?
It's my first event like this. — Is it? You seem very relaxed.

sayIt.instructions: Say Priya's lines. Record yourself, then listen back. Does your voice go up on Have you? Do you sound interested?
lines: Hi there. It's busy tonight, isn't it?
Have you? What line of work are you in?
Really? Then we've got something in common. I do the marketing for Oakline Furniture.
That makes sense. Anyway, I mustn't keep you from the food. Have you got a business card?

spot.instructions: Look at these lines from the conversation. The first four use a small word that steers the talk. The last two are questions, but they are not really asking for information.
examples: Mind you, they're very well made.
Granted, the rents are higher here. But there's far more work.
Anyway, I mustn't keep you from the food.
spot.question: Which word corrects gently? Which adds a but? Which agrees before arguing on? Which moves the talk on? And what are the last two questions for?
spot.answer: Actually corrects gently: Priya thinks Tomasz knows Kwame, and he doesn't. Mind you adds a but and keeps the compliment standing. Granted agrees that rents are higher, then but brings the real point. Anyway moves the conversation on. Isn't it? is a tag: Priya expects agreement, so it opens the conversation. Have you? is an echo question: it shows interest.

rules.title: Words that steer: actually, mind you, granted, anyway
rule: Actually corrects gently, or adds a surprise: I'm not in sales, actually. I'm in logistics.
Mind you adds a but and keeps your first point standing: It's a great venue. Mind you, it's a bit loud.
Granted agrees with part of a point before you argue on: Granted, it's expensive. But it saves time.
Anyway moves the talk on, or back to the main topic: Anyway, what brings you here?
They belong to speech and friendly messages. In a formal report, use however or in fact.
rules.mistake: Actually does not mean at the moment. Not: Actually, I live in Leeds (meaning these days). Say: At the moment, I'm living in Leeds.

rules.title: Question tags and echo questions
rule: A tag checks something or invites agreement. Positive sentence, negative tag: It's busy, isn't it?
Negative sentence, positive tag: You don't know Kwame, do you?
The tag uses the sentence's helping verb, or do, does or did: You came from Leeds, didn't you?
Voice down on the tag: you are fairly sure. Voice up: you really want to know.
An echo question shows interest: I've just moved. Have you? She works for Oakline. Does she?
rules.mistake: Not: You work with Kwame, isn't it? Say: You work with Kwame, don't you? The tag must match the verb.

practice.why: A positive sentence with is takes a negative tag: isn't it?
A negative sentence takes a positive tag, and present simple uses do.

practice.q: You came across the event online, ___ ?
practice.why: Came is past simple, so the tag uses did: didn't you?

practice.q: A: I've just moved here from Leeds. B: ___ ? What made you move?
practice.why: The echo question repeats the helping verb: I've moved, so Have you?

practice.q: The food's lovely. ___ , there isn't much of it.
practice.why: Mind you adds a but without taking back the first point.

practice.q: A: You work in sales, don't you? B: No, I'm in logistics, ___ .
practice.why: Actually corrects what someone thought, gently.

practice.q: ___ , the rent is higher here. But there's far more work.
practice.why: Granted agrees with part of a point, and but brings your own point.

practice.q: So that's why I left the bank. ___ , enough about me. What do you do?
practice.why: Anyway moves the conversation on, here from you to the other person.
A negative sentence with hasn't takes a positive tag: has she?

practice.q: A: My sister works for Oakline too. B: ___ ? Which department?
practice.why: Works is present simple, so the echo question uses does.

yourTurn.prompt: Someone at an event says: “Networking is a waste of time. Nobody here is really interested in you.” Answer them in three or four sentences. Agree with part of what they say, add a but, and move the talk on. Use granted, mind you, actually or anyway, and end with a tag or a question.
yourTurn.model: Granted, some people only want to sell you something. But I've met two of my best clients at events like this. Mind you, it took me a while to feel comfortable. Anyway, you came tonight, so it can't be that bad, can it?

text.title: Why the kettle matters
text.body:
By Lena Fischer
PRACTICE TEXT: the writer and the company are invented.

Ask people what they think of small talk, and many will tell you they hate it. Why talk about the weather when there is real work to do? But a growing number of managers believe that those two minutes by the kettle are not wasted at all.

Small talk is how colleagues start to trust each other. A casual chat about a football match or a weekend away tells you something about the person behind the job title. Once you know a little about someone, it is easier to ask them for help, or to tell them that something has gone wrong. For many people, these chats are also one of the small pleasures of working life.

This matters more than ever now that so many teams are remote. When everyone works from home, there is no queue at the coffee machine and no chat in the lift. Online meetings start on time and finish on time, with no conversation before or after. Many remote workers say they feel isolated, even when they are busy all day. What they miss is not the office itself, but the sense of belonging that came with it.

Some companies now plan for this. At Larkfield Software, the first ten minutes of every team call are for anything except work. “It felt strange at first,” says team leader Omar Haddad. “Now it's the part people enjoy most, and new staff bond with the team much faster.”

Small talk is a skill, and it can be learned. Face to face, eye contact and open body language show that you are listening. On a video call, a question about something in the background can put a nervous colleague at ease. Above all, be genuine: ask a question, listen to the answer, then ask about something they said.

So next time you meet someone new at work, don't rush back to your desk. And if you enjoyed the conversation, drop them a line afterwards. It takes a minute, and it is often the start of a good working relationship.

gist.q: What is the main point of the article?
gist.a: Small talk helps colleagues trust each other and feel part of a team.
wrong: Small talk wastes time that should be spent working.
Remote workers should go back to the office.
gist.why: The writer says small talk is how colleagues start to trust each other, and it gives people a sense of belonging.

detail.q: According to the article, what do many remote workers miss?
detail.a: the sense of belonging that came with the office
detail.why: The article says: What they miss is not the office itself, but the sense of belonging that came with it.

detail.q: What happens in the first ten minutes of Larkfield's team calls?
detail.a: People talk about anything except work.
wrong: The team leader explains the day's tasks.
New staff introduce themselves one by one.
detail.why: The first ten minutes of every team call are for anything except work.

detail.q: How can you put a nervous colleague at ease on a video call?
detail.a: Ask about something in the background.
wrong: Keep the call as short as possible.
detail.why: The article says a question about something in the background can put a nervous colleague at ease.

detail.q: What does the writer suggest you do after a good conversation?
detail.a: send the person a short message
wrong: go straight back to your desk
invite them to a team call
detail.why: She says: drop them a line afterwards. That means write them a short message.

items.meaning: Light, polite conversation about everyday things, such as the weather, the weekend or the journey in.
items.example: We made small talk about the traffic while we waited for the meeting to start.

items.meaning: Relaxed and informal, not planned or serious.
items.example: It was just a casual chat by the coffee machine, but it really helped.

items.meaning: To develop a close, trusting relationship with someone, often by sharing an experience.
items.example: The new team bonded quickly during the training week.

items.meaning: Working or done from home or another place, not in the office, using the internet.
items.example: Half of our team is remote, so most meetings happen on video.

items.meaning: Alone and cut off from other people, so you feel lonely.
items.example: Working from home all week made him feel isolated.

items.meaning: The feeling that people accept you and that you are part of a group.
items.example: Regular team lunches give new staff a sense of belonging.

items.meaning: Looking straight at the face of the person you are talking to, to show that you are listening.
items.example: Good eye contact makes you look confident in an interview.

items.meaning: The messages you send with your face, your hands and the way you sit or stand, without speaking.
items.example: His body language said he was bored, even though he kept smiling.

items.meaning: To help someone feel relaxed and less nervous.
items.example: The interviewer put me at ease by talking about the weather first.

items.meaning: Enjoyment, or something that you enjoy. People also use it in polite phrases when they meet or help someone.
items.example: It was a pleasure to meet you last night.

items.meaning: To write someone a short, informal message or email.
items.example: Drop me a line when you're back from your holiday.

model.title: A follow-up message
model.body:
Subject: Great to meet you last night

Hi Tomasz,

It was a pleasure to meet you at Kwame's event last night. I hope the move from Leeds is going well.

As I mentioned, Oakline is looking for a new delivery partner for our shops in the north. Your firm sounds like a good fit, and you already know our sofas!

Would you be free for a quick call next week? Tuesday or Wednesday morning would suit me best.

Best wishes,
Priya Sharma
Marketing Manager, Oakline Furniture

write.task: Write a follow-up message to someone you met recently, at work, at an event or anywhere else. It can be real or made up. Write 60 to 100 words. Say where you met, mention something you talked about, and suggest a next step.
write.starter: Hi …, It was a pleasure to meet you at …
checklist: I said where and when we met.
I mentioned something we talked about, so they remember me.
I suggested one clear next step: a call, a coffee or a meeting.
The tone is friendly, and the message is short.

card.title: Networking in the live class
card.situation: Your live class is a networking event. Everyone is there to meet new people. You don't know anyone well, and you want to leave with at least one useful contact.
card.goal: Meet three people. Start each conversation, find one thing you have in common, and arrange to follow up.

phrases: Hi, I don't think we've met. I'm …
So, how do you know the organiser?
What line of work are you in?
Really? Then we've got something in common.
Anyway, I mustn't keep you. Have you got a business card?
I'll drop you a line next week.
prepare.notes: Write three questions you can ask anyone, and one fact about yourself that could start a longer conversation: your job, a place you know well, or an interest.

doIt.liveClass: In the live class, the room is a networking event. Move from person to person, or from breakout room to breakout room. Talk to three people for about three minutes each, find something you have in common, and arrange to follow up.
doIt.wehel: Let's role-play a networking event. You are someone I have never met. Choose your own name, job and town, but don't tell me. I will start the conversation. Answer my questions, ask me some too, and give me chances to find something we have in common. If I stop talking, wait for me. At the end, tell me one phrase I used well and one I could improve.

model.title: Meeting someone new
lines: You
Hi, I don't think we've met. I'm Carlos.
Amina
Hello, Carlos. I'm Amina. It's quite a crowd tonight, isn't it?
You
It is. So, how do you know Mei?
Amina
We're on the same course, actually. I'm training to be an accountant.
You
Are you? I'm in finance too. I work for a bank in the city centre.
Amina
Really? So we've got something in common. Do you enjoy it?
You
Most of the time. Granted, the hours are long. But the people are great.
Amina
That's what I'm hoping for. Mind you, I'm still at the exam stage.
You
I remember that stage well! Anyway, I mustn't keep you. Have you got a business card?
Amina
Not yet, but here's my number. I'd be glad of some advice about banks.
You
Of course. I'll drop you a line next week, and we can meet for a coffee.
Amina
That would be lovely. It's been great to meet you.
compare: Did you introduce yourself and ask an easy first question?
Did you find something you have in common?
Did you use a word that steers, like actually, mind you, granted or anyway?
Did you arrange a clear next step before you said goodbye?

canDo: I can start a conversation with someone I don't know.
I can keep a conversation going with questions, tags and echo questions.
I can steer a conversation with actually, mind you, granted and anyway.
I can write a friendly follow-up message to someone I met.
I can meet new people at an event and arrange to follow up.

reading.before: Look at the title and the first page. Who is meeting whom, and where? What do you think they will find they have in common?
reading.talk: Which person in the text is best at keeping a conversation going, and how do they do it? Write three or four sentences, or talk about it with Wehel.

quiz.why: You're means you are, so the tag is aren't you?

quiz.q: A: I grew up in Nairobi. B: ___ ? So did I!
quiz.why: Grew is past simple, so the echo question uses did.

quiz.q: We met through a ___ friend. We both know Kwame.
quiz.why: A mutual friend is someone you both know.

quiz.q: Her name rings a ___ . Have we met before?
quiz.why: If a name rings a bell, it seems familiar.

quiz.q: Working from home every day made Lena feel ___ .
quiz.why: Isolated means alone and cut off from other people.

quiz.q: What does “I'll drop you a line” mean?
options: I'll send you a short message.
quiz.a: I'll send you a short message.
quiz.why: To drop someone a line is to write them a short, informal message.

quiz.q: A: It's too expensive. B: ___ , it's not cheap. But it will save us hours every week.
quiz.why: Granted agrees with part of the point before B argues on with but.

quiz.q: Half the team is away, so we need to ___ the meeting until next week.
quiz.why: To put something off is to move it to a later time.

quiz.q: If I ___ a car, I'd give you a lift to the station.
quiz.why: If + past, would + verb: a situation that is not true now. Never put would after if.

quiz.q: I didn't fix the car myself. I ___ at a garage.
quiz.why: Have + object + past participle: someone else did the work for you.

liveClass: Day 1: practise the networking conversation in pairs, then change the jobs and the places. Then a tag chain: each learner says a sentence about the room, and the next learner adds a tag or an echo question.

Day 2: the task. The live class is a networking event: each learner meets three people, finds something in common and arranges to follow up. Finish with each learner saying one thing they have in common with someone.
Day 3: talk about the book and answer questions. Then two learners read their follow-up messages aloud, and the class suggests one improvement for each.
